proposals.before: Song: Wei Zi Qi, younger brother of King Zhou by a concubine. First enfeoffment.
proposals.after: Song: Wei Zi Qi, elder brother of King Zhou by a concubine. First enfeoffment.
proposals.reason: Chinese 庶兄 means elder half-brother by a secondary consort, not younger brother.

proposals.before: Song Wei Zi Qi, Zhou younger brother by concubine. First enfeoffed.
proposals.after: Song Wei Zi Qi, Zhou elder brother by concubine. First enfeoffed.
proposals.reason: Chinese 庶兄 is elder half-brother; literal English wrongly has younger.

proposals.before: Qi was born wise, Yao established him as Minister of Rites, and gave him the surname Zi.
proposals.after: Qi was born wise, Yao established him as Minister of the Multitudes (Situ), and gave him the surname Zi.
proposals.reason: 司徒 is Situ (Minister of the Multitudes/Masses), not Minister of Rites (which would be 宗伯/禮官).

proposals.before: Qi born wise, Yao established as Minister of Rites, surnamed him Zi clan.
proposals.after: Qi born wise, Yao established as Minister of the Multitudes (Situ), surnamed him Zi clan.
proposals.reason: Literal English inherits the same office mistranslation of 司徒 as Rites.
黮 is read tán (Tan), not Meng; the English personal name mismatches the Chinese characters.
Literal field repeats the wrong reading Meng for 黮.

proposals.before: Speaking in terms of the Three Dynasties genealogical transmissions, Hou Ji had a father named Emperor Ku (Gaoxin);
proposals.after: Speaking in terms of the Three Dynasties genealogical transmissions, Hou Ji had a father named Gaoxin;
proposals.reason: Chinese only has 高辛; inserting Emperor Ku is an interpretive addition not in this unit.

proposals.before: Emperor Ku (Gaoxin) was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor.
proposals.after: Gaoxin was the great-grandson of the Yellow Emperor.
proposals.reason: Chinese names only 高辛; Emperor Ku is not in the source clause.
茲 here is glossed in the next sentence as 益大; literal 'this' obscures the etymological point carried by the idiomatic rendering.

decisions.reason: In 宋微子啟，紂庶兄, 庶兄 means elder half-brother by a secondary consort; the before wrongly has younger brother, and the after restores that kinship correctly.
The same 庶兄 in s111 requires elder, not younger, in the literal field; the after correctly replaces younger with elder without other change.
堯立為司徒 names the office 司徒 (Situ, Minister of the Multitudes), not rites; Minister of Rites would be 宗伯/禮官, so the after is the accurate rendering.
Literal likewise mistranslates 司徒 as Minister of Rites; replacing with Minister of the Multitudes (Situ) matches the Chinese office title.
The cell is 熊黮; 黮 is read tán, so Xiong Tan is the correct English name and Xiong Meng mismatches the characters.
Literal repeats the same wrong Meng reading for 黮; Xiong Tan is the correct reading of 熊黮.
后稷有父名高辛 names only 高辛; Emperor Ku is an interpretive insertion absent from this unit, and the after keeps the source name alone.
高辛，黃帝曾孫 likewise has only 高辛; stripping the inserted Emperor Ku restores the clause without changing the great-grandson claim.
子者茲 is immediately glossed as 茲，益大也, so 茲 here carries the 'increase' sense (滋), not demonstrative 'this'; the after matches that etymological gloss.

claimRetractions.reason: Accepted r0007 shows Emperor Ku / 帝嚳 was introduced only by the bad idiomatic of s0088; the Chinese names solely 高辛 and supplies no support for this title claim.
